module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Prime Triplet Conjecture

*Reference:* [Prime Triplet Wikipedia Page](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_triplet#Conjecture_on_prime_triplets)
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace PrimeTriplets

/--
Are there infinitely many tuples of three consecutive primes $(p, q, r)$ such that $r - p = 6$?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem prime_triplets :
    answer(sorry) ↔ {p : ℕ | Prime p ∧ (Prime (p + 2) ∨ Prime (p + 4)) ∧ Prime (p + 6)}.Infinite := by
  sorry

end PrimeTriplets

reformulations.difference: Lean counts initial primes p satisfying the two offset patterns, rather than explicitly counting triples of consecutive primes with first-to-last difference six. Consecutiveness is not separately imposed.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Every qualifying p is at least 5. Parity forces any prime strictly between p and p+6 to be p+2 or p+4. These cannot both be prime: one of p, p+2, p+4 is divisible by 3, and all exceed 3. Thus the condition determines a unique middle prime and gives three consecutive primes. Conversely, every consecutive prime triple with span six has one of these two patterns. Projection to the first member is therefore a bijection between the triples and the stated set, preserving infinitude. Both the pointwise equivalence and the infinitude equivalence were proved in /workspace/review/scratch.lean, without using the conjecture or sorry.

The research-open category agrees with the consulted sources. Checked the answer slot's type and scope, the equivalence of generic Prime and Nat.Prime, and Set.Infinite semantics. Lean tests exclude p = 0,1,2,3,4 and produce the initial members 5,7,11,13,17,37,41,67,97,101,103,107 below 120, matching Wikipedia. The scratch file compiles successfully, and its equivalence proofs have no sorryAx dependency. The reviewed file is unchanged.
